nameStory: The Atlantic rock crab gets its straightforward name from where it lives — among the rocky shores and rocky bottoms of the Atlantic Ocean. It's also called the "peekytoe crab" in fancy restaurants, a marketing name that comes from the pointed tips of its walking legs that look like tiny toes peeking out.
description: The Atlantic rock crab is a medium-sized crab with a smooth, oval shell that's wider than it is long. These sturdy crabs can grow up to about 5 inches across their shell, making them smaller than the lobsters they share their rocky homes with. Their shells are typically yellowish-brown with darker spots, and they have the classic crab body plan with eight walking legs plus two large claws for grabbing food and defending themselves. You'll find them scuttling around rocky areas from shallow tide pools down to surprisingly deep waters.

idTips.label: Shell shape and texture
idTips.description: The shell (carapace) feels smooth to the touch and is distinctly oval-shaped, wider than long, with a slightly domed surface that lacks the bumps or ridges found on some other crabs

idTips.label: Size and proportions
idTips.description: Reaches up to 5 inches across the shell, with claws that are moderately sized relative to the body — not dramatically oversized like some crab species

idTips.label: Shell coloration
idTips.description: Yellowish-brown to reddish-brown base color with darker brown or purplish spots scattered across the shell, creating a mottled appearance that helps them blend with rocky surfaces

idTips.label: Walking legs
idTips.description: Eight relatively slender walking legs with pointed tips that give a delicate appearance, ending in sharp points that help them grip rocky surfaces

idTips.label: Shell edge details
idTips.description: The front edge of the shell has small, rounded teeth or lobes that feel slightly rough when you run your finger along them

habitat: Look for Atlantic rock crabs in rocky intertidal zones, tide pools, and rocky bottoms along New England's coast from Maine to Connecticut. They prefer areas with plenty of rocks, boulders, and crevices where they can hide, from shallow tide pools you can explore at low tide down to deeper offshore waters. They're often found alongside green sea urchins, blue mussels, and rockweed in these rocky marine environments.

seasonality.spring: More active as waters warm, often seen moving around tide pools during spring low tides. This is when they begin emerging from deeper winter refuges.
seasonality.summer: Most active and easiest to spot during summer low tides, when they're feeding actively and may be seen out in the open on rocky surfaces or in shallow pools.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to deeper waters. Fall storms may wash some individuals into unusual intertidal spots where they're easier to find.
seasonality.winter: Much less visible as they move to deeper waters and become less active in cold temperatures, though some may still be found in deeper tide pools during extreme low tides.

funFact: Atlantic rock crabs are incredibly depth-versatile — while you might spot one in a shallow tide pool during your beach walk, their relatives are living nearly half a mile underwater at depths of 2,600 feet, making them one of the most depth-adaptable crabs in New England waters.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Jonah crab, which shares the same rocky habitats. Remember: Atlantic rock crabs have smooth, oval shells and more delicate-looking legs, while Jonah crabs have rougher, more rectangular shells with heavy-duty, chunky claws and a more robust build overall.
contextualKnowledge: You might see these sold in restaurants as "peekytoe crab" — a marketing term invented in the 1990s to make this previously overlooked species sound more appealing to diners. The name comes from their pointed leg tips, though most restaurant-goers have no idea they're eating the same crabs they might see scuttling around Maine tide pools.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Jonah crab, the Atlantic rock crab has a much smoother, more oval shell versus the Jonah crab's rougher, more rectangular shell. Atlantic rock crabs also have more proportionate claws and more delicate-looking legs, while Jonah crabs are built like little tanks with heavy, robust claws that look oversized for their bodies.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Atlantic Rock crab, the Jonah crab is generally more robust and heavy-bodied with a rougher shell texture.
